questions.stem: Which statement best captures the difference between mental health and mental illness?
options: mental health is simply the absence of illness; mental illness is any negative emotion
mental health is mainly physical; mental illness is mainly caused by social factors
mental illness affects everyone at times; mental health is rare and hard to reach
everyone has some level of mental health; a mental illness is a diagnosable disorder
questions.explanation: Mental health includes our emotional, psychological and social wellbeing and is something every person has to some degree. A mental illness is a diagnosable condition that significantly disrupts thinking, feeling or behaviour. Ordinary negative emotions are part of life and are not illnesses.

questions.stem: Sam has a diagnosed anxiety disorder that is well managed. He has close friends, enjoys his work and feels his life has purpose. Which statement is best supported?
options: Sam's diagnosis must be wrong, because he clearly functions well in daily life
good mental health always means that no illness is present at all
a person can have a mental illness and still have good mental health
Sam cannot have good mental health while his diagnosis remains
questions.explanation: Mental health and mental illness are related but separate: a person with a diagnosed illness can still experience wellbeing, meaning and good relationships. Treating them as opposite ends of one line wrongly implies that any diagnosis rules out good mental health.

questions.stem: Lena has never had a mental illness, but she feels flat, disengaged and without purpose most of the time. Which term best describes her state?
options: resilient
mentally ill
languishing
flourishing
questions.explanation: Languishing describes low positive mental health without a mental illness: the person is not ill but is not functioning or feeling well either. Flourishing is the opposite, combining feeling good with functioning well.

questions.stem: Feeling sad for a few weeks after a much-loved pet dies is best described as:
options: a sign of low resilience that needs immediate clinical treatment
an absence of mental health, because wellbeing has dropped
a normal emotional response that is not by itself a mental illness
a mental illness, because the person has been experiencing a low mood
questions.explanation: Sadness after a loss is a normal part of life and reflects changes in wellbeing, not illness. A mental illness involves symptoms that are more severe, longer lasting and significantly disruptive to daily functioning.

questions.stem: In earlier centuries, behaviours now recognised as symptoms of mental illness were often blamed on moral weakness or evil spirits. What does this best show?
options: people in the past had no concept of emotional or psychological wellbeing
ideas about mental illness reflect the beliefs of a time and culture
mental illnesses were much rarer in the past than they are in the present
modern ideas about mental illness will never change as new evidence appears
questions.explanation: How mental health and mental illness are understood depends on the beliefs, knowledge and values of a society, which change over time and differ between cultures. Current concepts may also change as evidence develops.

questions.stem: In the biopsychosocial approach, getting enough sleep each night is a factor in which dimension of wellbeing?
options: biological
psychological
sociocultural
spiritual
questions.explanation: Sleep affects the body's functioning, including brain chemistry and energy, so it is a biological factor. Psychological factors involve thoughts and emotions, and sociocultural factors involve relationships and the wider social environment.

questions.stem: Classify these factors in Harry's wellbeing: an optimistic thinking style; belonging to a community choir; regular physical activity.
options: psychological; sociocultural; biological
biological; psychological; sociocultural
sociocultural; biological; psychological
psychological; biological; sociocultural
questions.explanation: Optimism is a way of thinking, so it is psychological. Belonging to a choir provides social connection, which is sociocultural. Physical activity affects the body, which is biological.

questions.stem: Which is the best example of a sociocultural contributor to resilience?
options: a habit of thinking flexibly and solving problems step by step
a belief that one's own actions can change outcomes
a supportive network of family, friends and community groups
a calm temperament and a well-regulated stress response
questions.explanation: Sociocultural contributors to resilience come from relationships and the social environment. A calm temperament and stress response are biological, while flexible thinking and an internal locus of control are psychological.

questions.stem: Optimism is thought to support health across biopsychosocial dimensions. Which explanation best reflects this?
options: optimists experience no stress, so their bodies are never physically aroused
optimism is purely genetic, so it affects health only through biology
optimists avoid thinking about their problems until the problems disappear
optimists tend to cope actively, look after their health and seek support
questions.explanation: Optimism links to active problem-focused coping (psychological), healthier behaviours and less prolonged stress responses (biological), and seeking social support (sociocultural). Optimists still experience stress; they tend to manage it more effectively.

questions.stem: A school wants to build students' resilience using a biopsychosocial approach. Which plan best fits?
options: a single poster campaign telling all students to think more positively about their exams
extra homework so that students become used to working under heavy pressure
medication offered to any student who reports feeling stressed during exams
sleep and exercise education, skills to challenge unhelpful thoughts, and peer mentoring
questions.explanation: A biopsychosocial approach targets all three dimensions: biological (sleep, exercise), psychological (cognitive skills) and sociocultural (peer support). The other plans address only one dimension, or none in a helpful way.

questions.stem: In positive psychology, 'flourishing' describes:
options: the complete absence of any stress or negative emotion in a person's life
recovery from a mental illness after successful treatment
positive mental health, combining feeling good with functioning well
a temporary feeling of pleasure after an enjoyable experience
questions.explanation: Flourishing is a descriptor of positive mental health in which a person both feels good and functions well in life. It is more than a passing pleasure and does not require a life without stress.

questions.stem: In Seligman's three routes to happiness, the 'good life' involves:
options: using your strengths in the service of something larger than yourself
having enough money and status to meet every one of your needs
using your signature strengths to become absorbed in what you do
maximising pleasure and positive emotions as often as possible
questions.explanation: The good life, or engaged life, comes from using one's signature strengths in work, relationships and leisure, leading to absorption and engagement. Maximising positive emotion is the pleasant life, and serving something larger than oneself is the meaningful life.

questions.stem: Rosa uses her kindness and leadership to run a weekend program helping refugee families settle into her town. Which of Seligman's routes to happiness does this best show?
options: the pleasant life
the good life
the comfortable life
the meaningful life
questions.explanation: The meaningful life involves using one's strengths to belong to and serve something bigger than oneself. Although Rosa uses her strengths, the key feature here is that they serve a cause beyond herself.

questions.stem: Seligman argued that the pleasant life on its own gives less lasting happiness than the other routes. Which reason supports this?
options: positive emotions become harmful to health when they are felt too often
pleasant experiences cannot be shared with other people
pleasures always lead to guilt, which cancels out happiness
people adapt to pleasures quickly, so their effect fades with repetition
questions.explanation: People habituate to pleasures, so the same enjoyable experience produces less positive emotion each time. Engagement and meaning are thought to give more lasting wellbeing. Positive emotions themselves are beneficial, not harmful.

questions.stem: After a fun afternoon with friends, Ivy comes up with far more creative ideas for her art project than usual. Which theory best explains this?
options: cognitive-mediational theory
the James-Lange theory
assertiveness theory
broaden-and-build theory
questions.explanation: Fredrickson's broaden-and-build theory proposes that positive emotions widen the range of thoughts and actions a person considers, which encourages creativity and exploration. Over time this builds lasting personal resources.

questions.stem: According to the broaden-and-build theory, how do negative and positive emotions differ in their effect on thinking?
options: both narrow attention, but negative emotions do so for a longer time
both widen attention, but positive emotions do so for a shorter time
negative emotions narrow attention to specific actions; positive ones widen it
negative emotions widen attention to many actions; positive ones narrow it
questions.explanation: Negative emotions such as fear narrow attention towards specific action tendencies, such as escape, which is useful in danger. Positive emotions broaden thinking and action, and the resources built this way, such as friendships and skills, last beyond the emotion.

questions.stem: In Seligman's PERMA model of wellbeing, the letters stand for:
options: positive emotion, engagement, relationships, meaning, accomplishment
pleasure, energy, resilience, mindfulness, achievement
positive emotion, effort, reflection, motivation, acceptance
purpose, engagement, respect, meaning, autonomy
questions.explanation: PERMA identifies five elements of wellbeing: Positive emotion, Engagement, Relationships, Meaning and Accomplishment. Each can be pursued for its own sake and contributes to flourishing.

questions.stem: Ari becomes so absorbed in coding a game that he loses track of time. Which PERMA element does this most clearly show?
options: engagement
accomplishment
meaning
relationships
questions.explanation: Engagement is deep absorption in an activity that uses one's strengths, often described as flow. Accomplishment would be the sense of achievement when the game is finished.

questions.stem: After months of training, Mei finishes her first half-marathon and feels proud of reaching her goal. Which PERMA element does this most clearly show?
options: meaning
positive emotion
accomplishment
engagement
questions.explanation: Accomplishment is pursuing and achieving goals and mastery. Although Mei feels proud, the element highlighted by reaching a goal after sustained effort is accomplishment.

questions.stem: Seligman's PERMA model was developed from his earlier three-routes theory of happiness. Which two elements did PERMA add?
options: relationships and accomplishment
positive emotion and engagement
engagement and meaning
meaning and positive emotion
questions.explanation: The three routes correspond to positive emotion (pleasant life), engagement (good life) and meaning (meaningful life). PERMA keeps these and adds positive relationships and accomplishment as separate elements of wellbeing.

questions.stem: In research on how people respond to a partner's or friend's good news, an active constructive response is one that:
options: shows genuine enthusiasm and asks questions about the good news
offers quiet, low-key support without showing much further interest
points out the problems or downsides of the good news
ignores the good news and turns attention to oneself
questions.explanation: An active constructive response is enthusiastic and engaged, helping the person savour the event. Quiet, low-key support is passive constructive, pointing out problems is active destructive, and ignoring the news is passive destructive.

questions.stem: Zoe tells her friend she has won a place in the school orchestra. Her friend says, 'Won't that take up all your study time? Your marks might drop.' Which response style is this?
options: passive destructive
active constructive
passive constructive
active destructive
questions.explanation: The friend engages actively with the news but undermines it by focusing on its downsides, which is active destructive. A passive destructive response would ignore the news altogether.

questions.stem: Leo tells his brother he passed his driving test. His brother replies, 'Guess what happened at my work today,' and starts his own story. Which response style is this?
options: active destructive
passive constructive
active constructive
passive destructive
questions.explanation: Ignoring the news and turning the conversation to oneself is passive destructive. It is passive because it does not engage with the event, and destructive because it dismisses it.

questions.stem: Which response style to a partner's good news is most strongly linked with relationship satisfaction, and why?
options: passive destructive, because it keeps attention on shared problems
active constructive, because shared enthusiasm builds trust
passive constructive, because calm support avoids overexcitement
active destructive, because honest criticism helps a partner improve
questions.explanation: Research by Gable and colleagues found that active constructive responding was linked with greater relationship satisfaction, intimacy and trust. Passive constructive responses, though not hostile, were not linked with these benefits.

questions.stem: Which statement is the best example of an assertive response?
options: 'You always ruin our plans. You're so selfish and never think of me.'
'It's fine, whatever works for you,' said while secretly feeling upset inside.
'Sure, change it again,' said with a sigh and an annoyed eye-roll.
'I feel frustrated when plans change late. Could you tell me a day ahead?'
questions.explanation: Assertiveness means expressing one's own feelings and needs honestly and directly while respecting the other person, often using 'I' statements. Blaming is aggressive, hiding one's feelings is passive, and sarcasm is passive-aggressive.

questions.stem: Assertiveness training is likely to improve close relationships mainly because it teaches people to:
options: express needs and feelings honestly while respecting others' rights
always agree with others so that conflict can be avoided
win arguments by speaking more forcefully and loudly than the other person
hide negative feelings so that relationships stay calm
questions.explanation: Assertive communication lets both people's needs be heard, which reduces resentment and supports problem-solving. Always agreeing or hiding feelings is passive, and overpowering others is aggressive.

questions.stem: The VIA Inventory of Strengths (VIA-IS) was created by Peterson and Seligman to measure:
options: a person's intelligence and reasoning
a person's risk of developing a phobia
a person's character strengths
a person's symptoms of mental illness
questions.explanation: The VIA-IS is a self-report questionnaire designed to operationalise the Character Strengths and Virtues (CSV) handbook by identifying a person's character strengths. It does not diagnose disorders or measure intelligence.

questions.stem: The Character Strengths and Virtues handbook classifies:
options: six character strengths grouped under 24 virtues
24 mental disorders grouped under six categories
ten personality traits grouped under five factors
24 character strengths grouped under six virtues
questions.explanation: Peterson and Seligman identified 24 character strengths, such as curiosity, kindness and perseverance, organised under six core virtues: wisdom, courage, humanity, justice, temperance and transcendence.

questions.stem: Which statement best contrasts the CSV with the DSM-5?
options: the CSV is used by clinicians to diagnose disorders; the DSM-5 is completed by the public
the CSV focuses on what is wrong with people; the DSM-5 focuses on what is right
the CSV places people in categories; the DSM-5 measures strengths on a continuum
the CSV classifies strengths everyone has to some degree; the DSM-5 classifies disorders
questions.explanation: The CSV was designed as a positive counterpart to the DSM: it describes strengths that all people possess in varying amounts, while the DSM-5 sets out criteria for diagnosing mental disorders. Their focus is the reverse of what the third option claims.

questions.stem: Which is a similarity between the CSV and the DSM-5?
options: both offer a common language for classifying psychological features
both are used mainly to decide whether a person needs medication
both were written to describe what is going wrong in a person's life
both are completed by the person as a short online questionnaire
questions.explanation: Both are classification systems that give professionals a common vocabulary: one for disorders and one for strengths. The DSM-5 is used by clinicians to diagnose, whereas strengths are usually measured by a self-report questionnaire such as the VIA-IS.

questions.stem: After completing the VIA-IS, Noah learns that curiosity and humour are among his signature strengths. How could this result best be used?
options: to rank Noah's character against that of his classmates and friends
to identify which of his weaknesses should be removed from his character
to find ways to use those strengths more often in study, work and daily life
to diagnose whether Noah has a mental illness that needs treatment
questions.explanation: The VIA-IS is used to identify signature strengths so a person can use them more often, which is linked with greater engagement and wellbeing. It is not a diagnostic tool and is designed to describe an individual's own profile.

questions.stem: A group of adults complete the VIA-IS twice, four months apart, and their scores on each strength are very similar. This is evidence of the VIA-IS's:
options: representativeness
test-retest reliability
external validity
content validity
questions.explanation: Reliability is consistency of measurement; similar scores on two occasions show test-retest reliability. Validity concerns whether a test measures what it claims to measure, which this result does not show.

questions.stem: Researchers find that people's VIA-IS scores agree closely with ratings of their character strengths made by friends and family. What does this mainly support?
options: the validity of the VIA-IS as a measure of character strengths
the test-retest reliability of the VIA-IS over several months
the claim that the six-virtue structure fits every culture
the use of the VIA-IS for diagnosing mental disorders
questions.explanation: Agreement between self-reports and independent ratings by others suggests the inventory measures what it claims to measure, which is evidence of validity. Test-retest reliability would need the same people tested twice over time.

questions.stem: Which is a valid criticism of the VIA-IS?
options: as a self-report measure, people may describe themselves too favourably
it identifies only weaknesses, so it cannot show a person's strengths
it can only be completed and scored by a trained psychiatrist
it diagnoses mental disorders without any clinical interview
questions.explanation: Because the VIA-IS relies on self-report, social desirability and limited self-insight can bias scores. Other criticisms are that statistical analyses do not always reproduce the six-virtue grouping and that the strengths may reflect particular cultural values.

questions.stem: Which activity is the best example of mindfulness?
options: planning tomorrow's tasks in detail while quickly eating breakfast at the bench
pushing away any unpleasant thoughts as soon as they appear
replaying an argument to work out what should have been said
eating slowly, noticing each taste, and gently returning when the mind wanders
questions.explanation: Mindfulness means paying attention on purpose to the present moment without judgement, and calmly bringing attention back when it drifts. Pushing thoughts away is suppression, and planning or replaying events takes attention away from the present.

questions.stem: In loving-kindness meditation, a person:
options: silently repeats wishes of goodwill towards themselves and others
focuses only on the physical sensation of each breath going in and out
imagines feared situations until anxiety reduces
writes down three things that went well each day
questions.explanation: Loving-kindness meditation directs feelings of warmth and goodwill towards oneself and then others, and is linked with increased positive emotion. Focusing on the breath describes focused-attention meditation.

questions.stem: Compared with traditional CBT, which mainly targets negative thoughts and problems, positive CBT focuses mainly on:
options: pairing feared stimuli with relaxation in a gradual fear hierarchy
using medication to correct imbalances in neurotransmitters
strengths, exceptions to problems and what is already working well
uncovering repressed childhood memories that cause present problems
questions.explanation: Positive CBT builds on clients' strengths and successes, asking what is going well and how to do more of it, with the aim of increasing wellbeing. Pairing feared stimuli with relaxation is systematic desensitisation.

questions.stem: A psychologist asks a client, 'Think of a day this week when you handled stress well. What did you do differently that day?' Which approach is this most typical of?
options: positive CBT
traditional cognitive restructuring
systematic desensitisation
mindfulness meditation
questions.explanation: Searching for exceptions, times when the problem was handled well, and building on them is typical of positive CBT. Traditional cognitive restructuring would instead examine and challenge the client's negative thoughts.

questions.stem: Each night for a week, Jo writes down three things that went well that day and why. What is the main aim of this exercise?
options: to record symptoms of illness so that a diagnosis can be made by a doctor later
to reduce engagement in daily activities so that stress drops
to increase gratitude and positive emotion by focusing on what went well
to identify negative thoughts so they can be challenged in therapy
questions.explanation: The 'three good things' exercise is a positive psychology intervention that trains attention towards positive events, and has been found to increase happiness. It is not used to diagnose or to identify negative thoughts.

questions.stem: How does mindfulness differ from positive CBT in the way it deals with thoughts?
options: both ignore thoughts and focus only on changing the body's physiological arousal level
mindfulness accepts thoughts without judging them; positive CBT redirects focus to strengths
mindfulness challenges thoughts as false; positive CBT accepts every thought without change
both aim to remove all negative thoughts permanently from a person's mind
questions.explanation: Mindfulness involves noticing thoughts and accepting them without trying to change them. Positive CBT actively shifts attention towards strengths, successes and solutions. Neither aims to remove negative thoughts permanently.
